newsitem.title: GERMANY: TENNIS-GRAF'S FATHER COULD AVOID JAIL AFTER TAX TRIAL.
newsitem.headline: TENNIS-GRAF'S FATHER COULD AVOID JAIL AFTER TAX TRIAL.

text.p: The father of the world's top tennis player Steffi Graf could escape with a fine and a suspended sentence on Friday when a court rules on whether he evaded millions of marks of tax on his daughter's earnings.

In one of the most publicised tax trials in German history, Peter Graf, 58, has been accused of concealing 19.2 million marks ($11.7 million) of German tax on his daughter's earnings betweeen 1989 and 1993.
Prosecutors say the former second-hand car salesman, who has run Steffi's financial affairs since she was an unknown teenager, should be jailed for six years and nine months.
But judge Joachim Plass has said he does not expect an "exorbitant" jail term.
Peter Graf, who has already spent 15 months in custody during the investigation and trial, should not be forced to spend more time behind bars, his lawyers argue.

"Prominent experts led Peter Graf, the amateur, onto the tax equivalent of the north face of the Eiger and then, as he was hanging there, abandoned him," said celebrity lawyer Franz Salditt, in his closing arguments last week.
Graf's lawyers have not denied that their client set out to evade up to six million marks ($3.7 million) of tax.
But they claim his own naivety, the negligence of his tax advisers and the authorities' failure to act much earlier all contributed to the fiasco.

The trial has revealed a complex web of money management where Graf has been accused of picking up cash in plastic bags at tournaments and then transferring millions of dollars into back accounts across the globe to dodge tax.
The trial has fascinated the German public, who have taken Steffi to their hearts since she shot up through the world tennis rankings in the mid-1980s.
She said she entrusted financial matters to her father from an early age and was unaware of the details of her earnings.

Defence lawyer Kurt Himmelsbach asked the court for a sentence short enough to be suspended, which means no more than two years, and offered the payment of a fine to reduce the length of the prison term.
If the court does award a suspended sentence then Graf could be free to leave the country and head for the family's luxurious second family home in Florida.

Himmelsbach accused the regional finance ministry in Graf's home state of Baden-Wuerttemberg of turning a blind eye to avoid a scandal and asked the court to also take into account that Graf had already paid back some 20 million marks ($12.2 million) of taxes.

He also noted that Steffi was one of the country's only top sports stars not to have left Germany for a tax haven abroad, unlike big names such as soccer hero Franz Beckenbauer and Formula One racing driver Michael Schumacher.

Graf's lawyers argued during the five-month trial that he was a weak man who was out of his depth and had been led astray. They cited an addiction to alcohol and tablets, and traumas including a highly-publicised affair with a nude model.
A penitent Graf said on Monday: "I will never forget this trial as long as I live, and I don't want to forget it."
Steffi, whose career earnings are estimated at more than 100 million marks ($61 million), is still under investigation and may face a fine after Friday's verdict.
While her father's future is being decided, she is likely to be in Australia training after she unexpectedly lost in the fourth round of the Australian Open on Sunday.
The women's number one has been suffering a fever since the defeat but said she hoped to start training soon in preparation for the Pan Pacific Open in Tokyo next week. ($1=1.64 Mark)
